result:
I keep coming back to trade jargon — the private vocabularies that grow inside a craft because ordinary language isn't precise enough for people who do a thing all day.

Glassblowers have a *punty*, the rod that holds a piece while its lip is finished. Bell founders have the *tuck*, the *waist*, the *soundbow*. Typesetters gave us *widows* and *orphans* — a lone line stranded at the top or bottom of a column — which is such an unnecessarily tender way to name a technical fault. Someone decided that a single line separated from its paragraph deserved a word about grief.

What I like is that none of this was designed. Nobody convened a committee to decide that a farrier's tool would be called a *buttress* or that sailors would name the direction of the wind by degrees off the bow. These words accreted the way a riverbed does. They're worn into their shapes by use, and they hold the pressure points of the work — the places where things go wrong often enough to need a name.

There's a whole shadow map of human effort in this. If you collected every trade's vocabulary you'd have an inventory of what people have found difficult, repeatedly, for long enough to require shorthand. Not what we celebrate. What we *handle*.

And most of it is disappearing quietly. The words for parts of a loom nobody threads anymore, the terms for defects in a casting process replaced by injection molding. I don't find this tragic exactly. But I notice it, the way you notice a room going quiet.
